questions.q: Which description best fits the WebSocket protocol?
choices: A bi-directional, full duplex communications protocol initiated over HTTP
A one-way server push protocol that runs alongside HTTP on a separate port
A stateless request/response protocol that replaces HTTP/1.1 keep-alive
A client-only polling mechanism that repeatedly sends HTTP requests
questions.explain: WebSockets are bi-directional and full duplex, and the connection starts with an HTTP handshake. They are often used for streaming data and other asynchronous traffic.

questions.q: WebSocket messages are transactional: each message the client sends has to be answered by exactly one server message before the next one can be sent.
questions.explain: Either side can send a WebSocket message at any time, and messages are not transactional. The request/response transaction model belongs to HTTP.

questions.q: Which of these are characteristics of WebSocket connections?
choices: They are typically long-lived
Messages can be sent in either direction at any time
The connection normally stays open and idle until the client or server has something to send
Each message requires a new HTTP request and response
Only the client may start sending messages
questions.explain: WebSocket connections are long-lived. Either side can send at any time, and the connection sits idle until there is a message to send. A separate request/response for each message is how HTTP works.

questions.q: In which situation are WebSockets particularly useful compared with plain HTTP?
choices: A real-time feed of financial data that needs low latency and server-initiated messages
Downloading a large static file once
Submitting a single HTML form and showing a confirmation page
Serving cacheable images through a CDN
questions.explain: WebSockets are especially useful when low latency or server-initiated messages are needed, such as real-time financial data feeds.

questions.q: What is the difference between the ws:// and wss:// schemes?
choices: wss establishes the WebSocket over an encrypted TLS connection; ws uses an unencrypted connection
wss is for server-to-client messages; ws is for client-to-server messages
ws uses WebSocket protocol version 13; wss uses an older version
wss requires a CSRF token in the handshake; ws does not
questions.explain: wss means WebSockets over TLS, so the connection is encrypted. ws is unencrypted.

questions.q: Fill in the blank. Client-side JavaScript opens a WebSocket connection with: var ws = new ______("wss://normal-website.com/chat");
questions.explain: WebSocket connections are normally created in client-side JavaScript with the WebSocket constructor, e.g. new WebSocket("wss://normal-website.com/chat").

questions.q: Once a WebSocket object `ws` is connected, which call sends a message from the browser?
choices: ws.send("Peter Wiener")
ws.post("Peter Wiener")
ws.write("Peter Wiener")
ws.emit("Peter Wiener")
questions.explain: The browser sends a WebSocket message with ws.send(...).

questions.q: WebSocket messages are limited to a fixed plain-text format, so structured data cannot be sent in them.
questions.explain: In principle, WebSocket messages can carry any content or data format. Modern applications often send structured data as JSON, e.g. {"user":"Hal Pline","content":"..."}.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code does a server return when it accepts a WebSocket handshake?
questions.explain: The server responds with HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols, plus Connection: Upgrade, Upgrade: websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Accept.

questions.q: Which headers in the handshake request and response show that the exchange is a WebSocket handshake?
choices: Connection and Upgrade
Host and Cookie
Content-Type and Content-Length
Origin and Referer
questions.explain: The Connection header (containing Upgrade) and the Upgrade: websocket header, in both the request and the response, mark this as a WebSocket handshake.

questions.q: The Sec-WebSocket-Version request header gives the protocol version the client wants to use. What value does it typically have?
questions.explain: Sec-WebSocket-Version is typically 13.

questions.q: What does the Sec-WebSocket-Accept response header contain, and why?
choices: A hash of the Sec-WebSocket-Key value concatenated with a string defined in the protocol spec, to prevent misleading responses from misconfigured servers or caching proxies
The user's session token re-encrypted with the server's key, to authenticate the connection
A CSRF token the client must include in every later WebSocket message
The list of message formats the server accepts, such as JSON or XML
questions.explain: Sec-WebSocket-Accept is a hash of the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key concatenated with a fixed string from the specification. Its purpose is to prevent misleading responses caused by misconfigured servers or caching proxies.

questions.q: The Sec-WebSocket-Key request header contains a Base64-encoded random value, which should be generated fresh for each handshake request.
questions.explain: Sec-WebSocket-Key is a Base64-encoded random value that should be randomly generated in each handshake request.

questions.q: The Sec-WebSocket-Key header is used for authentication and session handling.
questions.explain: Sec-WebSocket-Key is a random value that prevents errors from caching proxies. It plays no part in authentication or session handling, and that is why it gives no CSRF protection.

questions.q: What happens to the network connection after a successful WebSocket handshake?
choices: It stays open and can carry WebSocket messages in either direction
It closes, and the client opens a new connection for each message
It stays open, but only the server may send on it
It is downgraded to plain HTTP once the first message is exchanged
questions.explain: After the 101 response, the connection stays open and is used for WebSocket messages in both directions.

questions.q: Which Burp Suite tool do you use to intercept and modify WebSocket messages on the fly?
choices: Burp Proxy
Burp Repeater
Burp Intruder
Burp Decoder
questions.explain: With interception turned on in Burp Proxy's Intercept tab, WebSocket messages from the browser or server are shown there so you can view or modify them, then click Forward.

questions.q: While browsing through Burp's browser, how can you tell that an application function uses WebSockets?
choices: Entries appear in the WebSockets history tab in Burp Proxy
The HTTP history shows responses with status 200 and a JSON body
Burp Repeater opens a new tab on its own
The browser's address bar changes to a ws:// URL
questions.explain: Use the application and watch for entries in Burp Proxy's WebSockets history tab.

questions.q: Which Burp Suite tool do you use to replay individual WebSocket messages and generate new ones?
choices: Burp Repeater
Burp Proxy's Intercept tab
Burp Comparer
Burp Sequencer
questions.explain: Send a message from the Proxy's WebSockets history or Intercept tab to Repeater. There you can edit it, send it repeatedly, or write new messages.

questions.q: In Burp Repeater, a new WebSocket message you write can be sent in either direction, to the client or to the server.
questions.explain: Repeater lets you enter a new message and send it to either the client or the server.

questions.q: The History panel in Burp Repeater only shows WebSocket messages you generated in Repeater.
questions.explain: The History panel shows every message sent over that WebSocket connection, including ones the browser or server generated. To modify one and send it again, use "Edit and resend".

questions.q: Which are reasons you might need to manipulate the WebSocket handshake rather than just the messages?
choices: It can let you reach more attack surface
An attack may drop the connection, so you need to establish a new one
Tokens or other data in the original handshake request may be stale and need updating
It is the only way to decrypt traffic sent over wss://
Messages cannot be edited once the connection is established
questions.explain: The material gives three reasons: reaching more attack surface, re-establishing a dropped connection, and refreshing stale tokens or data in the handshake. Messages can be edited after connection, using Proxy or Repeater.

questions.q: The pencil-icon wizard next to the WebSocket URL in Burp Repeater lets you attach to, clone, or reconnect a WebSocket. Which options show the full handshake request so you can edit it before connecting?
choices: Cloning a connected WebSocket or reconnecting to a disconnected WebSocket
Only attaching to an existing connected WebSocket
All three options, including attaching to an existing connection
None of them; the handshake can only be edited in the Proxy Intercept tab
questions.explain: Clone and reconnect show the full handshake request for editing. After that, "Connect" performs the handshake you configured. Attaching reuses a connection that is already established.

questions.q: In Burp Proxy, how do you choose whether client-to-server messages, server-to-client messages, or both are intercepted?
choices: Through the WebSocket interception rules in the Settings dialog
Through the Sec-WebSocket-Version header in the handshake
Through Repeater's History panel
You can't; Burp always intercepts both directions
questions.explain: Which directions get intercepted is set by the WebSocket interception rules in Burp's Settings dialog.

questions.q: A chat app sends {"message":"Hello Carlos"} over a WebSocket. The server relays the text to another user, whose browser renders it as Hello Carlos, with no other input processing or defenses. Which message is a proof-of-concept XSS attack?
choices: {"message":""}
{"message":"' OR 1=1--"}
{"message":"Hello Carlos","admin":true}
{"message":"../../etc/passwd"}
questions.explain: The message is inserted into the other user's page as HTML, so an tag with an onerror handler runs JavaScript in their browser. This is XSS delivered over WebSockets.

questions.q: Which vulnerabilities can come from user-supplied input sent to the server over WebSockets being processed in unsafe ways?
choices: SQL injection
XML external entity (XXE) injection
Cross-site scripting, when attacker data is relayed to other users
None; WebSocket traffic is immune to injection because it isn't HTTP
questions.explain: Practically any web vulnerability that arises with HTTP can also arise with WebSockets. Unsafe server-side processing can cause SQL injection or XXE. Attacker data relayed to other users can cause XSS or other client-side vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Some blind vulnerabilities reached through WebSockets produce no visible response. Which kind of technique may be the only way to detect them?
choices: Out-of-band (OAST) techniques
Comparing Sec-WebSocket-Accept values
Downgrading the connection from wss to ws
Replaying the handshake with a new Sec-WebSocket-Key
questions.explain: Some blind vulnerabilities reached via WebSockets may only be detectable with out-of-band application security testing (OAST) techniques.

questions.q: Most input-based vulnerabilities affecting WebSockets can be found and exploited by tampering with the contents of WebSocket messages.
questions.explain: Most input-based WebSocket vulnerabilities are found by tampering with message contents. Some design flaws, though, can only be reached by manipulating the handshake.

questions.q: Which design flaws can typically only be found and exploited by manipulating the WebSocket handshake?
choices: Misplaced trust in HTTP headers such as X-Forwarded-For when making security decisions
Flaws in session handling mechanisms
Attack surface introduced by custom HTTP headers the application uses
Stored XSS in chat message contents
SQL injection in a JSON field of a WebSocket message
questions.explain: Handshake-level flaws include misplaced trust in headers like X-Forwarded-For, session handling flaws, and custom-header attack surface. XSS and SQL injection in message bodies are found by tampering with the messages.

questions.q: What generally determines the session context in which WebSocket messages are processed?
choices: The session context of the handshake message
A session token included in every individual WebSocket message
The Sec-WebSocket-Accept value returned by the server
The IP address of the client sending each message
questions.explain: Messages are generally processed in the session context set by the handshake. This makes flaws in handshake session handling significant, and it is also what cross-site WebSocket hijacking exploits.

questions.q: Name an HTTP header that the material gives as an example of misplaced trust when an application makes security decisions based on the WebSocket handshake.
questions.explain: Trusting the X-Forwarded-For header (for example, to decide a client's IP address) in the handshake is a design flaw that can be exploited by manipulating the handshake.

questions.q: Which are recommended guidelines for securing a WebSocket connection?
choices: Use the wss:// protocol (WebSockets over TLS)
Hard code the URL of the WebSockets endpoint and never include user-controllable data in it
Protect the WebSocket handshake message against CSRF
Treat data received over the WebSocket as untrusted in both directions
Rely on the Sec-WebSocket-Key header to authenticate the user
Use ws:// for lower latency, since the handshake already runs over HTTP
questions.explain: The guidelines are to use wss://, hard code the endpoint URL with no user-controllable data, protect the handshake against CSRF, and handle data safely on both client and server. Sec-WebSocket-Key provides no authentication.

questions.q: Data that the client receives from the server over a WebSocket can be trusted and inserted into the page directly, because only client-to-server data needs validation.
questions.explain: Data received over a WebSocket should be treated as untrusted in both directions. Server-to-client messages can carry attacker-controlled data, such as relayed chat messages, which can lead to XSS.

questions.q: Which measure specifically prevents cross-site WebSocket hijacking?
choices: Protecting the WebSocket handshake against CSRF, e.g. with a CSRF token or other unpredictable value
Using a longer Sec-WebSocket-Key
Sending all messages as JSON instead of plain text
Setting Sec-WebSocket-Version to the latest version
questions.explain: CSWSH is CSRF on the handshake. The defense is to protect the handshake against CSRF so it doesn't rely solely on cookies.

questions.q: Why should the WebSocket endpoint URL be hard coded rather than built from user-controllable data?
choices: So an attacker can't control which endpoint the client connects to
Because WebSocket URLs can't contain query strings
Because the server checks the URL against Sec-WebSocket-Accept
So the connection uses ws:// instead of wss://
questions.explain: The guideline is to hard code the endpoint URL and never incorporate user-controllable data into it. Otherwise an attacker could influence where the client's WebSocket connects.

questions.q: What is cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH) essentially?
choices: A cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability on the WebSocket handshake
A stored XSS vulnerability in WebSocket message contents
A man-in-the-middle attack on unencrypted ws:// traffic
Guessing another user's Sec-WebSocket-Key
questions.explain: CSWSH (also called cross-origin WebSocket hijacking) is a CSRF vulnerability on the WebSocket handshake.

questions.q: Under what condition does a WebSocket handshake become vulnerable to cross-site WebSocket hijacking?
choices: It relies solely on HTTP cookies for session handling and contains no CSRF tokens or other unpredictable values
It uses ws:// instead of wss://
It uses Sec-WebSocket-Version 13
The server returns 101 Switching Protocols
questions.explain: CSWSH arises when the handshake depends only on cookies for session handling and has no CSRF token or other unpredictable value, so a cross-site page can make it on the victim's behalf.

questions.q: What makes cross-site WebSocket hijacking more powerful than regular CSRF?
choices: The attacker gets two-way interaction: they can send messages and also read the server's responses
It works even when the victim is not logged in to the target application
It gives the attacker the victim's session cookie value
It lets the attacker execute code on the server directly
questions.explain: Regular CSRF can only trigger actions. In CSWSH the attacker's page can also read messages the server sends back over the hijacked connection, so sensitive data can be captured.

questions.q: What can a successful cross-site WebSocket hijacking attack often let an attacker do?
choices: Perform unauthorized actions while masquerading as the victim user
Retrieve sensitive data that the victim user can access
Decrypt the victim's previously recorded wss:// traffic
Change the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value the server computes for other users
questions.explain: If the app performs sensitive actions based on client messages, the attacker can trigger them. If it returns sensitive data in server messages, the attacker can capture it.

questions.q: In a CSWSH attack, where does the malicious WebSocket connection come from, and in whose session context does the application handle it?
choices: From a malicious page on the attacker's own domain, visited by the victim, and handled in the victim's session
From the attacker's own browser, handled in the attacker's session
From the vulnerable application's own page, handled anonymously
From a caching proxy, handled in the proxy's session
questions.explain: The attacker hosts a page on their own domain that opens a cross-site WebSocket connection to the vulnerable app. The victim's browser sends its cookies, so the app handles the connection in the victim's session.

questions.q: A handshake containing a random Sec-WebSocket-Key value is protected against cross-site WebSocket hijacking, because that value is unpredictable.
questions.explain: Sec-WebSocket-Key exists to prevent errors from caching proxies and is not used for authentication or session handling. A handshake whose only session token is a cookie is probably vulnerable even though it has a Sec-WebSocket-Key.

questions.q: What is the first step in performing a cross-site WebSocket hijacking attack?
choices: Review the application's WebSocket handshakes and determine whether they are protected against CSRF
Find an XSS vulnerability in WebSocket message contents
Obtain the victim's session cookie
Downgrade the target's wss:// connection to ws://
questions.explain: CSWSH is CSRF on the handshake, so you start by checking whether the handshakes are protected against CSRF, looking for ones that rely only on cookies.

questions.q: Once the attacker's page has opened a hijacked WebSocket to the vulnerable site, what might the rest of the attack involve? (It depends on the application's logic.)
choices: Sending WebSocket messages to perform unauthorized actions on behalf of the victim
Sending WebSocket messages to retrieve sensitive data
Simply waiting for incoming messages that contain sensitive data
Reading the victim's cookies out of the handshake response
questions.explain: Depending on how the app uses WebSockets, the attacker sends messages to trigger actions, sends messages to request data, or just waits for sensitive messages to arrive.

questions.q: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking is also known as cross-origin WebSocket hijacking.
questions.explain: Both names refer to the same attack: CSRF on the WebSocket handshake.
